query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding minor amounts (about 0.2–0.5 at.% each) of Y and Hf to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will stabilize its grain boundaries and phase interfaces, reduce grain coarsening during thermal cycling, lower room‐temperature creep rate, and enhance corrosion resistance—all without degrading its inherent strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring a uniform, fine lamellar fcc/B2 (or L12/B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled microalloying additions of 0.2–0.5 at.% Y and Hf via conventional melting and casting methods.
generation.conditions: Evaluate performance under cyclic thermal fluctuations (e.g., thermal cycling between –40°C and 700°C), under long-term mechanical loading to assess creep (using accelerated room-temperature creep tests), and in corrosive environments (chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions) that mimic aerospace fastener conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The reactive elements will segregate to grain boundaries and phase interfaces, lowering their energy and acting as diffusion barriers to suppress grain growth. This segregation will also promote the formation of a more stable and adherent protective oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: The minor additions of Y and Hf reduce grain boundary energy and inhibit boundary migration, retarding microstructural coarsening under high temperatures and cyclic thermal conditions. Simultaneously, they improve the integrity of the protective oxide scale, thereby decreasing corrosion rate, while maintaining the fine lamellar architecture necessary for high strength and ductility. This dual effect also helps to reduce the rate of room-temperature creep by limiting the diffusion paths at the grain boundaries under sustained mechanical load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the doped alloy is expected to exhibit approximately 15–20% improved creep resistance, reduced grain coarsening during thermal cycling (e.g., ~10–15% smaller grain size increase), and more robust corrosion resistance (as indicated by lower corrosion current densities in electrochemical tests), while retaining the excellent strength–ductility balance inherent to the lamellar structure.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, undoped AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with its established lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated when the additions are kept low (≤1 at.% total) to preserve the lamellar structure. The tested conditions should not exceed temperatures where phase transformations occur beyond stabilization limits (~700°C) and the corrosive environments should be representative of chloride-rich acid solutions encountered in aerospace applications.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal concentrations of Y and Hf might require fine-tuning to avoid potential embrittlement or interference with the lamellar morphology. Long-term cyclic performance under actual service conditions and potential scale-up issues may introduce variability. Additionally, interactions with other minor impurities or processing parameters could affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: the control (undoped AlCoCrFeNi2.1) and the experimental alloy doped with 0.2–0.5 at.% Y and Hf. Subject both sets to (1) thermal cycling tests (e.g., 1000 cycles between –40°C and 700°C), (2) accelerated room-temperature creep tests under a constant load, and (3) electrochemical corrosion tests using chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions to simulate aerospace conditions. Characterize the microstructure pre- and post-treatment using SEM/TEM and evaluate mechanical properties through tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size and phase stability via SEM/TEM imaging quantification before and after thermal cycles
Creep strain versus time curves under constant load
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization measurements to assess corrosion resistance
Tensile stress–strain characteristics to confirm retention of strength–ductility balance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., less than 10% enhancement in creep resistance or corrosion resistance) relative to the control, or if the lamellar microstructure degrades (evidenced by excessive grain coarsening or loss of phase integrity), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this work, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and co-doping Y and Hf AlCoCrFeNi2.1 YHf-EHEA coatings were successfully prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. 1. The YHf co-doping did not alter the solidification microstructure and phase structure of the EHEA coating. The microstructure morphologies of the top and bottom portions of coatings were composed of cellular and columnar dendrites, respectively. And the phase structure consisted of FCC and BCC/B2. 2. After heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h, the BCC/B2 structure was relatively stable in all coatings while the nanoscale Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC. 3. papers.title: Enhanced strength-ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae.
papers.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing that preserves the inherited fine lamellar structure to produce an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure with hierarchical heterogeneities.
papers.findings: Achieved a superior combination of strength and ductility compared to conventional single-phase HEAs and even traditional TRIP/TWIP steels. The lamellar geometry enabled two-hierarchical constraint effect and microcrack-arresting mechanisms.
papers.mechanism: The inherited lamellar structure facilitates strain partitioning, promoting back-stress strengthening and dislocation storage while arresting microcracks.

papers.title: Thermal Stability and Hot Corrosion Performance of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 High-Entropy Alloy Coating by Laser Cladding.
papers.approach: Laser cladding of both a base EHEA and a Y and Hf co-doped variant (YHf-EHEA)
papers.findings: While the microstructure (FCC and BCC/B2 phases) remained similar, the YHf co-doped coating showed improved thermal stability (smaller grain growth upon heat treatment) and enhanced resistance to hot corrosion scale spallation.
papers.mechanism: The minor alloying additions (Y and Hf) stabilize the microstructure by reducing grain boundary energy and inhibiting coarsening; they also improve the adhesion and integrity of the protective oxide scale.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.approach: Electrochemical measurements and surface characterization in chloride-containing sulfuric acid, at various temperatures
papers.findings: At elevated temperatures, the passive film becomes unstable with a narrower passive range and significant pitting, especially on the B2 phase. The alloy shows good passivation at low temperatures but deteriorates under higher temperature conditions.
papers.mechanism: Temperature alters the composition (hydroxide/oxide balance) of the passive film, making it more susceptible to Cl⁻ attack and localized dissolution.

papers.title: Influence of ordered L1₍₂₎ precipitation on strain-rate dependent mechanical behavior in a eutectic high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Al₀.₇CoCrFeNi (a variant related to AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁) with a lamellar dual-phase fcc/B2 structure
papers.approach: Low-temperature annealing to precipitate nano-scale ordered L1₍₂₎ (L12) precipitates within the fcc phase
papers.findings: The precipitation of L12 significantly increased the yield strength (by ~200–310 MPa) under quasi-static loading without a major loss in ductility, and maintained high work hardening ability.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via the introduction of coherent nanoparticles that impede dislocation motion (via Orowan bowing and bypassing), enhancing resistance without severely compromising deformation.

papers.title: Dynamic Shear Deformation of a Precipitation Hardened Al₀.₇CoCrFeNi Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy Using Hat-Shaped Specimen Geometry.
papers.system: Al₀.₇CoCrFeNi eutectic HEA with manipulated microstructure via precipitation hardening (L12 re-precipitation)
papers.approach: Comparison between a benchmark heat-treated state (HTA with fcc/B2 phases) and an aged condition (HTA-580 with fcc + L12 and B2 + bcc phases) through quasi-static and dynamic shear tests
papers.findings: The aged (HTA-580) condition demonstrated about a 200 MPa increase in yield strength along with reduced deformation zone around adiabatic shear bands during dynamic testing, indicating improved localized mechanical response.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation of nano-scale L12 phase provides additional strengthening by hindering shear localization and modifying dislocation behavior at the lamellar interfaces.

papers.title: Nanostructuring with Structural-Compositional Dual Heterogeneities Enhances Strength-Ductility Synergy in Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Hybrid processing combining cryo-rolling and warm-rolling to produce a microstructure with dual heterogeneities (retained lamellar regions coexisting with nanocrystalline transformed regions)
papers.findings: The resultant dual heterogeneous microstructure led to an unprecedented combination of high strength (~2000 MPa) with moderate ductility (~8%), ascribed to significant back-stress strengthening and enhanced dislocation storage.
papers.mechanism: The stored cryogenic deformation energy accelerates phase transformations during subsequent warm deformation; the resulting strain gradients and heterogeneous hardness facilitate both strength and ductility.

papers.title: Phase-selective recrystallization makes eutectic high-entropy alloys ultra-ductile.
papers.approach: A novel processing concept triggering phase-selective recrystallization to achieve a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded within a rigid hard phase skeleton
papers.findings: Produced an EHEA with ultra-high ductility (≈35% uniform elongation) and very high true stress (≈2 GPa), effectively unlocking latent strain hardening capacity.
papers.mechanism: Selective recrystallization in the soft phase eliminates weak interfaces, allowing sustained strain hardening and delaying early crack initiation.

established: Eutectic HEAs can combine high strength (from hard phases like B2) and good ductility (from ductile FCC/L12 phases) via a lamellar microstructure.
Thermo-mechanical processing and controlled precipitation can significantly enhance the strength–ductility balance.
Corrosion and high-temperature performance depend sensitively on passive film stability, which deteriorates with temperature.

approaches_tried.approach: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling, warm-rolling, annealing) to develop hierarchical or dual-phase microstructures.
approaches_tried.outcome: Marked improvements in strength and ductility through enhanced back-stress and dislocation storage mechanisms, though challenges remain under extreme environmental conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Precipitation strengthening via low-temperature annealing to form nano-scale ordered L12 precipitates.
approaches_tried.outcome: Increased yield strength (by ~200–310 MPa) while largely maintaining ductility; effective under both quasi-static and dynamic loading.

approaches_tried.approach: Microalloying/co-doping with Y and Hf in laser-clad coatings.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced thermal stability and hot corrosion resistance due to reduced grain coarsening and improved oxide scale adhesion.

mechanisms: Inherited lamellar microstructure promotes strain partitioning, back-stress strengthening, and microcrack-arresting.
Precipitation strengthening achieved through coherent nano-scale L12 particles impeding dislocation motion.
Doping (e.g., Y and Hf) stabilizes microstructure and enhances the integrity of protective oxide scales in corrosive environments, reducing scale spallation.
Phase-selective recrystallization improves ductility by eliminating weak interfaces and enabling full strain hardening.
disagreements: There is some debate regarding the trade-offs introduced by precipitation strengthening; while L12 precipitates raise yield strength, potential reductions in ductility or changes in strain rate sensitivity are noted in some studies.

The relative importance of microstructural features (e.g., lamellar spacing, phase boundary characteristics) versus chemical modifications (e.g., doping) in performing under extreme environments remains under discussion.
open_questions: How can a single intervention be optimized to simultaneously improve long-term mechanical stability (including creep resistance), high-temperature performance, and corrosion resistance in EHEAs?
What is the optimal balance between precipitation strengthening and microalloying to achieve resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations without compromising ductility?
How do phase boundary behaviors and microstructural stability evolve under prolonged mechanical loading and in corrosive environments?
What processing parameters (e.g., cooling rates, deformation conditions) would best preserve beneficial lamellar structures at industrially relevant sample sizes?
opportunities: Investigate a combined approach that integrates minor microalloying additions (such as Y and Hf) with controlled thermo-mechanical processing to lock in a stable lamellar microstructure that resists coarsening, creep, and corrosion at high temperatures.
Explore the use of selective precipitation (e.g., inducing L12 particles) concurrently with microalloying to optimize both mechanical strength and environmental stability.
Develop and test large-scale processing routes that mimic laboratory-scale improvements, specifically targeting the aggressive conditions of aerospace fasteners.

Undertake systematic studies on the evolution of passive films and phase boundary integrity under cyclic temperature fluctuations and sustained load to better inform alloy design for extreme environments.

directions.direction: Microalloying with reactive elements (Y and Hf) to stabilize interfaces
directions.assessment: Directly targets the deficiencies—the grain boundary instability, high-temperature coarsening, creep under long-term loading, and corrosion—by promoting grain boundary and oxide-scale stabilization. Prior work on Y/Hf co‐doped coatings (e.g. PMC10488378) shows reduced grain growth and improved corrosion resistance. This intervention respects the lamellar structure and is feasible with controlled small additions.

directions.direction: Controlled precipitation processing (low-temperature annealing to form L12 nanoprecipitates)
directions.assessment: Addresses strength via precipitation strengthening (as shown in PMC6478865) but does not directly target the creep and corrosion issues. Although effective for yield strength improvement, the method might affect ductility and not fully mitigate degradation under extreme temperatures.

directions.direction: Surface modification via applying protective coatings (e.g., laser cladding)
directions.assessment: Enhances corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior and is proven in coating studies (PMC10488378). However, it is an additional processing step rather than an intrinsic improvement to the bulk alloy’s creep and long-term load-bearing capability.

directions.direction: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing to refine the microstructure further (e.g., cryo-rolling followed by annealing)
directions.assessment: This can enhance the strength–ductility synergy (as seen in cryo-rolling studies PMC5818523) but may not fully address environmental stability, creep, and corrosion challenges inherent in applications like aircraft fasteners.

directions.direction: Modeling-simulation studies to optimize the lamellar spacing and phase boundary characteristics
directions.assessment: While useful to understand the effects of microstructural parameters on mechanical behavior, this approach is indirect. It does not provide an immediate single intervention that improves operational performance under extreme conditions.

choice.direction: Microalloying with reactive elements (Y and Hf) to stabilize interfaces
choice.why: This intervention directly improves the layered alloy’s performance by reducing grain-boundary energy, retarding grain coarsening, and promoting the formation of protective, adherent oxide scales. Evidence from Y and Hf co-doping in EHEA coatings (PMC10488378) supports improved thermal stability and hot corrosion resistance. It is achievable as a single compositional modification that maintains the beneficial lamellar microstructure, while also potentially mitigating creep and ensuring stability under prolonged mechanical loading and temperature fluctuations.
